Music is provided by the organizers at standardized tempos — waltz at 28-30 bars per minute, samba at 50-52.
Costume rules are strict by age: juvenile couples face restrictions on dress, rhinestones, and makeup to keep the sport age-appropriate.
Age categories run from juvenile through junior, youth, adult, and senior divisions, each with its own minimum ages.
equipment: Latin shoes
Open, flexible, suede-soled with a flared heel for women — $60-150.
Standard shoes
Closed court shoes for men, satin pumps with a lower heel for women — $80-200.
Practice wear
Comfortable training clothing and practice skirts — $30-100 per piece.
Competition dresses and tailsuits
A stone-set Latin dress runs $300-1,500; men's tailsuits $300-1,000, usually resold and rebuilt over a career.
Floor
Sprung wooden floors are the standard; studios rent practice space by the hour at $10-25.
Hair, tan, and accessories
The finishing economy of the sport — professional competition prep costs $50-200 per event.
training: Technique is built alone: solo basics and body isolation drills before partner work, every session.
Condition like a 90-second sprinter — Latin rounds are glycolytic, so interval work with 90-second to two-minute efforts matches the demand.
Build strength for frame and power: core anti-rotation work, glute and calf work for Standard's rise, and shoulder endurance for the hold.
Cross-train ballet for Standard lines and a strength discipline for Latin speed — the top couples typically do.
Rehearse full competition simulations: five dances in sequence with short breaks, several times a week before a championship.
Protect the feet: calf stretching, blister care, and rotation between heel heights prevent the overuse injuries that end careers.
pathway: Studio classes
Social ballroom and first medal tests — most careers start in a beginner class, child or adult.
Local and national circuit
Medalist and open competitions by age group; couples climb through championship tiers.
National squad and ranking
WDSF world-ranking events and national team selection in the amateur ranks.
Professional titles
WDC-affiliated professional championships and the Blackpool professional events.
Coaching and adjudication
Fellowship qualifications and judging licenses extend careers past competition.
events: Blackpool Dance Festival
The British Open at the Winter Gardens, annually in late May and June since 1920 — the sport's most coveted title.
WDSF World Championships
Annual world titles across Standard, Latin, 10 Dance, and formation for amateur couples.
UK Open Championships
Each January in Bournemouth — the season's first major and a Blackpool predictor.
International Championships
London each October — the other historic major on the English circuit.
Asian Games
Dancesport in the program every four years since 2010 — the discipline's multi-sport showcase.
WDSF GrandSlam
The premier annual ranking series, hosted across the continents.
legends: Donnie Burns and Gaynor Fairweather
Scotland — a record fourteen World Professional Latin titles from 1984 into the 1990s; still the benchmark.
Marcus and Karen Hilton
England — the Standard dynasty of the 1980s and 1990s, with multiple world and British Open titles.
Bryan Watson and Carmen Vincelj
The Latin athletes of their era — nine World Professional Latin titles between them.
Mirko Gozzoli and Edita Daniute
Multiple World Professional Standard champions whose style defined the 2000s and early 2010s.
Riccardo Cocchi and Yulia Zagoruychenko
The dominant World Professional Latin couple of the 2010s, with a decade of world titles.
getting_started: Book one private lesson and one group class a week at a reputable studio — ballroom is partner-skill heavy and self-teaching has a ceiling.
Buy proper shoes early; sneakers ruin Latin hip action and Standard footwork.
Learn the five basic figures of waltz and cha-cha before anything flashy — basics are what judges actually score.
Practice at home to competition-tempo music, ten minutes per dance, counting aloud.
Enter a medal test or a beginner competition within three months; rounds teach more than months of lessons.
Watch Blackpool finals on video — six couples, five dances, a masterclass in every one.
Stretch hips and calves daily; the sport asks for range the couch does not.
glossary: Frame
The held upper-body structure connecting partners — Standard's invisible engine.
Rise and fall
The vertical swell through waltz and foxtrot steps.
Cuban motion
The Latin hip action produced by knee and weight transfer.
Skatings system
The majority-based final marking method that converts judges' placements into results.
Line of dance
The counterclockwise traffic direction every Standard dance follows.
Closed hold
The Standard embrace, maintained throughout the dance by rule.
Open figure
A pattern where partners separate — legal in Latin, restricted in Standard.
10 Dance
The championship format requiring all five Standard and all five Latin dances.
Amalgamation
A linked sequence of figures rehearsed as one phrase.
Walk-on
The final couples' entrance parade — the sport's version of a title-fight walkout.

name: Capoeira
tagline: A fight that dances — music, cunning, and acrobatics inside Brazil's circle of drummers.
overview: Capoeira is the Afro-Brazilian discipline that plays a fight as a game: two capoeiristas trade evasive kicks, sweeps, and acrobatics inside the roda, a circle of musicians and singers led by the berimbau. It is at once martial art, dance, and ritual — trained with the body and the voice together.

Born among enslaved Africans in Brazil and criminalized for decades, capoeira survived through mestres who shaped it into teachable schools — Mestre Bimba's faster Regional and Mestre Pastinha's traditional Angola. UNESCO inscribed the roda of capoeira as intangible cultural heritage in 2014, and academies from Salvador to Seoul keep the music as central as the movement.

Newcomers should know the ginga comes first: the swaying base step from which every attack and escape grows. Capoeira is learned as a conversation — you do not win a roda, you play it well — and the music, the Portuguese songs, and the etiquette of the circle are half the art.
facts: Developed by enslaved Africans in Brazil from the 1500s onward, drawing on Central African movement traditions
A national sport of Brazil by declaration, with the roda inscribed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage in 2014
Mestre Bimba's Regional (1930s) and Mestre Pastinha's Angola (1941) define the art's poles
A circle of players, singers, and a bateria of berimbau, atabaque, and pandeiro — the berimbau leads
Modern groups mark rank with a cordao or corda, awarded at annual batizados
Ladainha, corridos, and rhythmic toques — Angola, Sao Bento Grande, Iuna — direct the game's tempo
Academies on every continent, with strong scenes in Brazil, Europe, North America, and Asia
history: Enslaved Africans in Brazil develop capoeira, blending Central African fight-dances with the realities of plantations and cities.
Brazil's new republican penal code bans capoeira by name; practitioners are jailed for decades.
Mestre Bimba opens his academy in Salvador and structures capoeira Regional — sequences, graduations, and a fighting identity.
After a demonstration before President Getulio Vargas, capoeira is legalized, and Bimba's school becomes a national reference.
Mestre Pastinha opens the Centro Esportivo de Capoeira Angola in Salvador, preserving the older, grounded game.
Mestres emigrate and academies open across the Americas, Europe, and Asia; films like Only the Strong (1993) widen the audience.
UNESCO inscribes the roda de capoeira on its intangible cultural heritage lists, formalizing global recognition.
formats: Capoeira Angola
The older game: slower, lower, closer, richer in malicia and trickery, played to a full bateria.
Capoeira Regional
Bimba's faster, more upright system with fixed training sequences and a clear martial structure.
Capoeira Contemporanea
The modern blend most groups teach — Regional energy and Angola cunning in one repertoire.
Maculele and folkloric performance
The stick-dance and staged shows that carry capoeira onto theater and festival stages.
Roda de rua
Street rodas in plazas and markets — the art's public face and its oldest stage.
skills: Ginga
The rhythmic sway-step that is capoeira's base — constant, low, and ready to become any move.
Three-minute ginga rounds daily, front and back; 100 repetitions to each side with a metronome until it breathes on its own.
Esquivas
The escape family — cocorinha, esquiva baixa, negativa — dodges that keep the head off the kick's line.
Partner drill: one kicks slowly, one escapes, then switch; 20 clean repetitions per esquiva per session.
Kicks
Meia lua de compasso, armada, queixada, martelo — circular and straight attacks launched from the ginga.
Slow-motion kicking against a hanging target for line and control; power comes after precision, never before.
Aus and acrobatics
The cartwheel family — au aberto, au fechado, au sem mao — plus macacos and flips for travel and escape.
Cartwheel drills on both sides against a wall first; acrobatics enter the roda only after landings are silent.
Rasteiras and sweeps
The ground game — rasteira, vingativa, tesoura — takedowns woven into the flow of play.
Practice from negativa positions with a patient partner at half speed; in the roda, sweeps are pulled by etiquette.
Music: berimbau and song
The single-stringed bow leads the bateria; singers answer in call-and-response.
Ten minutes of berimbau daily — one toque at first — and memorize one corrido per week.
Malicia
The cunning layer — feints, pauses, chamadas, and the reading of an opponent's intent.
Play slow games with masters and watch: rodas teach malicia faster than drills ever will.
rules: The roda has no scoring: the game is judged by the mestre, the audience, and the players themselves on rhythm, trickery, and control.
The bateria leads — the berimbau sets the toque, and the game must follow the music's tempo and character.
Attacks are controlled: hard kicks are pulled at head level, and contact is the exception that ends a game, not its goal.
The ladainha opens formal rodas — a solo song, often by the mestre, that sets the story and the pace.
A chamada is a ritual pause — one player offers a call, the other answers; refusing one breaks the game's etiquette.
Regional training uses Bimba's fixed sequences of attack and response, teaching timing before free play.
Entry follows ritual: players buy the game (comprar o jogo) at the foot of the berimbau, and cutting in carelessly is a genuine offense.
equipment: Berimbau
Biriba stick, wire string, and cabaca gourd with a caxixi shaker — $40-150 handmade.
Atabaque
The tall hand drum that drives the roda; a good one runs $150-500.
Pandeiro and agogo
Tambourine and double bell — $20-60 each, and the cheapest way into the music.
Abada
White training pants worn tied at the waist — $30-60.
Cordao
The graduation cord or ribbon, colored by group tradition and awarded at the batizado.
Training space
A smooth floor and room to cartwheel; academies carry the roda, and a home corner needs only about three square meters.
training: Ginga endurance is the base: capoeira games are interval work, so train repeated two-to-three-minute rounds with rolling recovery.
Build the ground game's strength — handstands, bridges, and bear crawls give the low game its engine.
Train flexibility for high kicks and low escapes: daily hip openers, hamstring work, and spinal mobility.
Play music daily — capoeira training is incomplete without berimbau, clapping, and song; the body follows the orchestra.
Rotate between Angola-style slow play and Regional-style speed; each teaches what the other hides.
Protect wrists and knees with progressive loading — cartwheel volume and low-game drills grow slowly over months.
pathway: First roda
Community classes and university groups introduce ginga, music, and the circle's etiquette.
Batizado
The annual baptism ceremony where new students receive their first cordao and play their first official games.
Graduado and instrutor
Mid-rank students begin teaching; many groups send them to lead academies abroad.
Contra-mestre and mestre
Decades of training, a reputation earned in rodas, and responsibility for a community's games and music.
International community
Workshops, encontros, and festivals connect groups across countries year-round.
events: Batizados and trocas de cordao
Annual graduation ceremonies in every major city, with rodas, guest mestres, and music that run all night.
Encontros and festivals
Group gatherings that draw mestres and students across borders, typically annually or semi-annually.
Rodas de rua
Public street rodas, scheduled weekly in cities from Salvador to Lisbon to New York.
Cultural festivals and performance seasons
Folkloric companies stage capoeira and maculele year-round, from Brazil's Carnival stages to world tours.
Ceremonial showcases
Capoeira featured in the Rio 2016 Olympic opening ceremony — recognition on the world stage without Olympic competition.
legends: Mestre Bimba
Manoel dos Reis Machado (1889-1974) — creator of capoeira Regional, whose 1930s academy legalized and professionalized the art.
Mestre Pastinha
Vicente Ferreira Pastinha (1889-1981) — guardian of capoeira Angola, whose 1941 academy kept the old game alive.
Mestre Joao Grande
Angola master of Pastinha's lineage who carried the traditional game to New York and taught it worldwide.
Mestre Joao Pequeno
Pastinha's heir in Salvador, who taught Angola into his nineties and shaped generations of masters.
Besouro Manganga
The legendary early-1900s capoeirista of Bahia — a folk hero whose escapes and audacity still fill the songs.
getting_started: Find a group that teaches music from day one — a capoeira class without berimbau is a fitness class in disguise.
Learn the ginga in front of a mirror: three minutes daily for a month makes it yours.
Sing — memorize one corrido in your first month; the voice is a training tool, not decoration.
Build the ground basics — cocorinha, negativa, au — before any acrobatics; cartwheels come with control, not courage.
Attend rodas as an audience first: watch how games start, pause, and end before you buy one.
Stretch hips and hamstrings 15 minutes daily; the low game demands range.
Expect sore wrists and puzzled neighbors — train on a mat, keep the volume humane, and stay for the music.
glossary: Roda
The circle of players, musicians, and singers where capoeira happens.
Ginga
The swaying base movement from which all attacks and escapes flow.
Berimbau
The single-stringed musical bow that leads the bateria and sets the game's tempo.
Bateria
The orchestra of instruments — berimbaus, atabaque, pandeiro, agogo, reco-reco.
Toque
A berimbau rhythm — Angola, Sao Bento Grande, Iuna — each dictating a style of game.
Malicia
Cunning — the feints, patience, and trickery that make capoeira a conversation, not a workout.
Jogo
The game played by two capoeiristas inside the roda.
Esquiva
An escape movement that evades a kick without leaving the game's rhythm.
Rasteira
The low sweep that takes a standing player off their feet.
Chamada
A ritual call within the game — a pause offered and answered before play resumes.
